title: Fractions
summary: Fractions name equal parts; operations work by matching, counting, or comparing those parts.
idea:
A fraction names equal parts of a whole. In `3/4`, the bottom number tells how many equal parts the whole is cut into. The top number tells how many of those parts are taken.

Equivalent fractions name the same amount with different-size parts. `1/2`, `2/4`, and `3/6` are the same amount. Multiplying or dividing the top and bottom by the same number keeps the amount the same.

For operations, keep the meaning of the parts visible. Adding needs same-size parts. Multiplying by a fraction means taking that fraction of something. Dividing asks how many of one amount fit into another.
why_it_works:
Fractions can be added only when the parts are the same size. For `1/2 + 1/3`, both fractions are rewritten in sixths. `1/2 + 1/3` becomes `3/6 + 2/6`, and `3/6 + 2/6` is `5/6`.

Multiplying a whole number by a fraction changes the count of parts, not the size of the parts. `3*(2/5)` becomes `(3*2)/5`, and `(3*2)/5` is `6/5`.

Dividing asks how many divisors fit. For `(2/3)/(3/4)`, turn over the divisor and multiply. `(2/3)/(3/4)` becomes `(2/3)*(4/3)`, `(2/3)*(4/3)` becomes `(2*4)/(3*3)`, and `(2*4)/(3*3)` is `8/9`.

explanations.why: The fractions have different-sized parts, so they cannot be counted together yet. Rewrite them as equivalent fractions with sixths.
explanations.another_way: Use a common denominator. `1/2` becomes `3/6`, and `1/3` becomes `2/6`.
explanations.visual: A bar shows `1/2` shaded in halves and `1/3` shaded in thirds, with parts not yet the same size.

explanations.why: Now both fractions use sixths, so the parts are the same size. Add by counting sixths.
explanations.another_way: Keep the denominator because the unit is still sixths. Add the top numbers in `3/6 + 2/6`.
explanations.visual: A bar cut into sixths shows `3/6` shaded, then `2/6` more shaded.

explanations.why: The total is five sixths, so `3/6 + 2/6` is `5/6`. This is the answer.
explanations.another_way: Count all the shaded sixths in the bar. There are five sixth-size parts.
explanations.visual: A bar cut into six equal parts has five parts shaded, showing `5/6`.

explanations.why: A whole number times a fraction means taking that many lots of the fraction. Here, `3*(2/5)` shows three lots of `2/5`.
explanations.another_way: Think of the multiplication as repeated groups of the same fraction.
explanations.visual: A bar split into fifths shows three groups, with two fifths shaded in each group.

explanations.why: Only the count of fifths changes. So `3*(2/5)` becomes `(3*2)/5`.
explanations.another_way: Keep the fifths as the size of the parts, and multiply how many of those parts are taken.
explanations.visual: The bar still uses fifth-size pieces, and the shaded count is shown as `3*2` fifths.

explanations.why: The multiplication in the top is carried out, so `(3*2)/5` becomes `6/5`. This is the answer because the expression is fully simplified from the given steps.
explanations.another_way: Count the shaded fifths: three groups of two fifths make `6/5`.
explanations.visual: One whole bar and one more fifth are shaded, for a total of `6/5`.

explanations.why: The expression `(2/3)/(3/4)` asks how many `3/4` parts fit into `2/3`. To divide by a fraction, change to multiplying by its reciprocal.
explanations.another_way: Think of division by `3/4` as measuring `2/3` in groups of size `3/4`. The reciprocal will be used in the next step.
explanations.visual: A bar shows `2/3` of a whole, with `3/4` of a whole marked as the size being counted.

explanations.why: The divisor has been flipped, so `(2/3)/(3/4)` becomes `(2/3)*(4/3)`. Now it is a multiplication of fractions.
explanations.another_way: Keep the first fraction and turn over the second fraction. Only the fraction being divided by changes.
explanations.visual: A bar model still shows `2/3` being measured by copies of `3/4`; the written work uses `4/3` for calculation.

explanations.why: To multiply fractions, multiply the tops and multiply the bottoms. So `(2/3)*(4/3)` becomes `(2*4)/(3*3)`.
explanations.another_way: This writes the product before carrying out the multiplication. The numerator factors and denominator factors are kept separate.
explanations.visual: A bar is split into `3*3` equal small parts, with `2*4` of those parts counted.

explanations.why: The products in `(2*4)/(3*3)` give `8/9`. This is the final value of the original division.
explanations.another_way: The answer `8/9` fits the comparison: the amount `2/3` is smaller than the part size `3/4`, so the quotient is less than a full copy.
explanations.visual: A bar model shows `8` of `9` equal parts shaded, representing `8/9`.

misconceptions.belief: To add fractions, add the tops and add the bottoms.
misconceptions.why_it_feels_right: It treats the fraction like two separate whole numbers, and it works the same way as multiplying fractions.

what_to_say.probe: Is your answer bigger or smaller than `1/2`? Should it be?
what_to_say.nudge: Can you add halves and thirds directly, or do you first need parts of the same size?
what_to_say.tell: Cut both into sixths: `3/6 + 2/6` is `5/6`. We only count the parts; their size stays the same.

misconceptions.source_quote: Some students add fractions by adding the tops and adding the bottoms.

misconceptions.belief: To multiply a fraction by a whole number, multiply both the top and the bottom.
misconceptions.why_it_feels_right: Students learned that doing the same to the top and the bottom is safe, from equivalent fractions.

what_to_say.probe: Is `6/15` more than `2/5`, less, or the same? What should three lots of `2/5` be?
what_to_say.nudge: Write three lots of two fifths as an addition and count the fifths.
what_to_say.tell: Three lots of two fifths is six fifths, `6/5`. Only the number of parts changes.

misconceptions.source_quote: Some students multiply both the top and the bottom by the whole number.

misconceptions.belief: When dividing fractions, turn over the first fraction.
misconceptions.why_it_feels_right: "Flip and multiply" is remembered as a slogan without which fraction is flipped.

what_to_say.probe: How many three quarters fit into two thirds: more than one, or less?
what_to_say.nudge: Which fraction are we counting with? That is the one to turn over.
what_to_say.tell: Only the divisor is turned over: `(2/3)*(4/3)` is `8/9`, a little less than one.

misconceptions.source_quote: Some students flip the first fraction when dividing, not the second.

misconceptions.belief: You can cancel a number on the top with the bottom even across a plus sign.
misconceptions.why_it_feels_right: Cancelling common numbers works for products, and the student sees a 2 on the top and a 2 on the bottom.

what_to_say.probe: What is the top of the fraction altogether, before you divide?
what_to_say.nudge: Work out the top first, then divide. Do you get the same answer?
what_to_say.tell: The fraction bar divides the whole top: `(2+4)/2` is `6/2`, which is `3`.

misconceptions.source_quote: Some students cancel across a plus sign.

misconceptions.belief: To simplify a fraction, you may divide just the top or just the bottom.
misconceptions.why_it_feels_right: Halving a number feels like simplifying, and the student does not check that the amount stays the same.

what_to_say.probe: Is `3/8` the same amount as `6/8`? Draw both as bars.
what_to_say.nudge: What number divides both the top and the bottom?
what_to_say.tell: Divide the top and the bottom by the same number: `6/8` is `3/4`.

misconceptions.source_quote: Some students simplify by changing only one part of the fraction.

questions.question: Why can’t we add the top numbers and the bottom numbers?
questions.answer: The bottom numbers name the size of the parts. Halves and thirds are different kinds of parts, so they must be rewritten as same-size parts before adding.

questions.question: Why does `1/2 + 1/3` become `3/6 + 2/6`?
questions.answer: Sixths can show both halves and thirds. `1/2` is `3/6`, and `1/3` is `2/6`, so the parts match before adding.

questions.question: What does the bottom number do?
questions.answer: It names the size of the equal parts. In `3/4`, the whole is cut into four equal parts.

questions.question: When multiplying `3*(2/5)`, why does only the top change?
questions.answer: There are three groups of two fifths. The number of fifths changes, but the size of each part is still fifths.

questions.question: Why do we flip the second fraction in division?
questions.answer: Division asks how many divisors fit. The divisor is the amount being counted, so the divisor is turned over before multiplying.

questions.question: How can students check a fraction answer?
questions.answer: Estimate first. Ask whether the answer should be more or less than `1/2`, or more or less than one. A quick bar model can also show if the result makes sense.

outline.title: Name the parts
outline.activity: Use a simple whole split into equal parts. Connect the bottom number to the size of the parts and the top number to the count of parts. Read `3/4` as three of four equal parts.

outline.title: Equivalent fractions
outline.activity: Show that `1/2`, `2/4`, and `3/6` name the same amount. Emphasize that multiplying or dividing the top and bottom by the same number keeps the value.

outline.title: Add with common parts
outline.activity: Work through `1/2 + 1/3`. Rewrite it as `3/6 + 2/6`, then combine the counts so `3/6 + 2/6` is `5/6`. Contrast with adding tops and bottoms.

outline.title: Multiply as groups of parts
outline.activity: Use `3*(2/5)`. Treat it as three lots of two fifths. Show `3*(2/5)` becomes `(3*2)/5`, and `(3*2)/5` is `6/5`.

outline.title: Divide as how many fit
outline.activity: Use `(2/3)/(3/4)`. Ask how many three-quarters fit into two thirds. Show `(2/3)/(3/4)` becomes `(2/3)*(4/3)`, then `(2*4)/(3*3)`, then `8/9`.

outline.title: Estimate and draw
outline.activity: Before calculating, ask whether an answer should be more or less than `1/2` or one. Use a bar model for any fraction calculation that feels uncertain.
